fact_sheet.business_description: Capital Cities is combining its broadcast and publishing operations with ABC, a national television network and related media properties [D01]. The business sells audiences to advertisers while supplying news and entertainment to viewers and readers [D01].
products_customers_and_why_they_buy: Broadcast and publishing products sold to advertisers and audiences; repeat purchase relies on established local positions and audience loyalty [D01]

earnings_record: Capital Cities standalone EPS grew from $5.38 in 1980 to $10.40 in 1984 [D02]; 1985 Q1 net income was $27.7m vs $27.1m in 1984 [D03]
competitive_position: Local media franchises possess defensible positions built on audience and advertising support; national network economics differ from local stations [D01, D06]

management_and_capital_allocation: Tom Murphy and Dan Burke have a long operating record using a low-cost, owner-oriented approach [D01]; minority structure of the ABC investment limits unilateral capital-allocation influence [D02]
price_and_valuation: Negotiated subscription price for 3 million shares at $172.50 per share [D02, D04]; standalone 1984 P/E 16.59x [D04]; no combined company P/E available [D04]

The value will reveal itself as this management team reduces costs and optimizes the network’s operations over time [D01].

final.memo:
Capital Cities is combining its high-quality broadcast and publishing assets with the ABC network, a transaction that unites significant media properties [D01]. We have long understood and admired this business model, which sells valuable audiences to advertisers through established local and national franchises [D01].

Tom Murphy and Dan Burke have built an extraordinary record, demonstrating consistent growth and high returns on equity [D02]. Their operating style is low-cost and intensely owner-oriented, which has served shareholders well in the past [D01].

However, we are required to act as investors, not merely admirers of management. At the current subscription price of $172.50, the initial earnings yield is approximately 6.03%, while long-term Treasury bonds offer 9.05% with far less risk [D04]. Paying a premium for the hope of future synergies, while accepting a yield significantly lower than the risk-free rate, does not meet our standard for a margin of safety [D04].

We remain cautious of the significant debt load incurred to finance this acquisition [D02]. Unless the debt can be serviced rapidly, the financial flexibility of the combined entity is constrained, and any failure in ABC's ratings could lead to a permanent impairment of capital [D02, D05]. We prefer to keep our cash and wait for opportunities that offer more certain returns relative to the current bond market [D04].
